source.title: Scalable next-scale autoregression for medical image generation across anatomical regions
source.authors: Zhi-Cheng He; Yun-Peng Zhao; Jun-De Wu; Zi-Wei Niu; Zi-Yue Wang; Bo-Han Li; Zi-Jun Li; Lan Lin; Nan Liu; Yue-Ming Jin

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses scalability and reports medical-image generation quality across MedVAR sizes, but it does not test the claim's language-model loss laws or fit a power law to a measure covered by the listed versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports FID across four MedVAR sizes, with semantic conditions alone and with semantic plus structural conditions. These are image-generation quality measurements, not held-out cross-entropy or a fitted power-law analysis; record them under fits_no_version. Diffusion comparisons, downstream tasks, tokenizer results, and other ablations do not test the listed scaling-law versions.
record.test_reason: The study reports image-generation FID for four MedVAR sizes, but never measures held-out loss against parameters, tokens or compute. It fits no power law, tests no extrapolation or compute-optimal allocation, and includes no fixed-size shape comparison. Kaplan et al. is cited only as motivation. FID also falls with size and training length together (240/240/300/350 epochs), so the size trend is confounded. This is a related construct, recorded under fits_no_version, not a test of V5's power-law form.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that generation quality improves with MedVAR size and call next-scale autoregression scalable. They make no power-law or compute-optimal claim, and they note that size and training duration varied together.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains a next-scale autoregressive medical image generator and evaluates FID, rather than measuring held-out language-model cross-entropy against parameter, token, or compute sweeps. Model size and training duration both vary; no power-law fit or compute-optimal allocation is reported.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported FID values differ between semantic-only and semantic-plus-structural conditioning; this is not a test of power-law fit sensitivity.

fits_no_version.finding: MedVAR FID falls monotonically with depth (16/20/24/30; 322M to 2,053M parameters). With semantic plus structural conditions it goes 10.87→10.15→9.78→9.31. With semantic conditions alone it goes 11.01→10.43→10.16→10.03, flattening at the largest size. Training epochs also rise with size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In a next-scale autoregressive medical image generator, larger models trained longer achieve lower FID, with diminishing gains.

record.problems: The size sweep reports point FID values without uncertainty for these comparisons and does not fit or test a power law. Model sizes also have different training durations: 240, 240, 300 and 350 epochs for depths 16, 20, 24 and 30, respectively. No compute-optimal allocation is tested.
record.rows_left_out: No additional model-size FID results were left out. Other reported metrics and experiments do not bear directly on the listed scaling-law versions.

untested.parts: No held-out cross-entropy sweep over parameters, tokens or compute.
No fit on small runs used to predict larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation of parameters versus data.
Depth and size vary together; there is no fixed-parameter shape comparison.
Only four FID points across image-model sizes, with no power-law fit and with training duration confounded with size.
Downstream segmentation and reconstruction use one generator, not a scale sweep.
No exponents or fitting choices are analysed.

record.verdict_notes: Rows are correctly linked to none. The discussion explicitly acknowledges that size and training duration were varied together. FID values are point estimates for the size sweep.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out language-model loss sweep over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run power-law fit or prediction of substantially larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token split.
No comparison isolating depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The study measures medical-image FID across model sizes, but does not test whether a power-law form holds in image generation or other modalities or training regimes.
Downstream segmentation and reconstruction are evaluated, but not as a scaling relationship with pretraining loss or model scale.
No fitted exponents, fit-method comparison, or compute-optimal split is analyzed.
